title: Development impacts on ancient woodlands in the United Kingdom—Collaborative identification of priority evidence and practice needs
content:
Development pressures on UK ancient woodlands are widespread and ongoing. This prompted a multi-sector expert consultation, which identified 12 priority research questions. Evidence gaps, diverse site contexts and policy implementation challenges require more targeted research, policy guidance and monitoring of outcomes to strengthen protection for ancient woodlands.


Abstract

Ancient woodlands in the UK face growing pressures from nearby development despite their recognition as ‘irreplaceable habitats’ with high biodiversity potential and cultural value. Effective mitigation is currently hindered by significant knowledge gaps around impacts from urbanisation, land use intensification and associated human activities on ancient woodland extent, condition and biodiversity. We used a multi-stakeholder, participatory approach to identify high-priority research questions to inform evidence-based conservation policy, practice and mitigation strategies for strengthening ancient woodland protection. We developed an online survey to gather questions and invited participation from 143 experts and their wider networks including practitioners, researchers and policymakers in the environment, planning and construction sectors. Submitted questions were discussed and ranked by a subset of experts during two in-person workshops, based on urgency, actionability, data needs and policy relevance. Qualitative data generated from workshop discussions were also analysed thematically to identify themes underpinning current policy, practice and research. Twelve priority research questions were identified. The highest-ranked question focuses on the effective width and composition of vegetated ‘buffer’ areas necessary to protect ancient woodlands from impacts while also providing ecological benefits. Three key themes characterise the current research, policy and practice landscape: (i) evidence gaps and data needs, (ii) ecological context dependency (the need for site-specific approaches) and (iii) challenges to policy implementation. Practical implications. Clearer, evidence-based guidance on protective vegetative buffers is needed, tailored to different development pressures and woodland contexts. Current evidence provides a partial foundation for guidance, but new research is required to address knowledge gaps. Consistent assessment of ancient woodland loss and deterioration depends on robust, repeatable condition monitoring before and after development. Monitoring and survey protocols should be standardised but site-adaptable, using appropriate condition indicators. Assessment and ongoing monitoring can also be improved with cross-organisational data sharing. Together with targeted research on impact pathways and mitigation effectiveness, these measures would substantially strengthen evidence-based protection of the UK's irreplaceable ancient woodlands.
